analysis.one_liner: Guarantees disabled people who qualify for institutional care the right to receive that care at home in their communities instead.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a senior Republican with 144 cosponsors from both parties, the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Disability Integration Act would make it illegal discrimination for states and insurers to force people with disabilities who need long-term help with daily living into nursing homes or institutions when they could live at home. States and insurers would have to offer community-based services before institutionalizing anyone, end waiting lists and cost caps on home care, ensure enough accessible affordable housing, and report yearly on progress, with a 12-year transition deadline and a small boost in federal Medicaid matching money for states that comply. People denied these services could sue in federal court, and the Justice Department could enforce the law and fine violators.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities who need long-term services and supports — including those now living in institutions and those at risk of being placed in one — gain a federal right to be served in their own homes and communities, plus the right to sue and win damages if denied. Their family caregivers also gain from new support requirements.

how_it_helps.text: States and insurers that fund institutional placements would be barred from denying community-based services, imposing waiting lists, cost caps, or payment structures that keep people out of the community, or requiring services to be delivered in congregate or disability-specific settings [S2] [S3].
Institutionalized individuals must be offered and notified of community-based alternatives, and community-based services must be offered before anyone is institutionalized [S2] [S3].

States would have to ensure enough affordable, accessible, integrated housing, assess transportation barriers, and plan transitions out of institutions with measurable annual targets, backed by a five-point increase in the federal Medicaid match for home and community-based services for complying states [S2] [S3].

Individuals could bring civil actions in federal court with appointed counsel, actual and punitive damages, and injunctions to prevent institutionalization, and the Attorney General could enforce the law and assess civil penalties up to $100,000 for a first violation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, which would have to shift Medicaid long-term care spending from institutions to home and community-based services over a 12-year transition and expand accessible housing. Nursing homes and other institutional providers would lose revenue as funding moves to community care, and private long-term care insurers would face new nondiscrimination requirements.

drawbacks.text: States would carry a large fiscal burden: the bill requires shifting funding from institutions to community-based services within 12 years, but its only dedicated new federal money is a five-percentage-point FMAP increase limited to specific home and community-based expenditures, so states and their taxpayers would absorb much of the remaining cost [S2] [S3].

The private right of action with damages and attorney's fees, plus civil penalties for public entities, would invite litigation against states during the transition and could be costly even where states are making good-faith progress [S3].

Supporters of the existing system would note that institutions provide round-the-clock care that some people with the most severe disabilities use by choice or necessity; the bill protects choice of setting but the funding shift it mandates could strain the institutional side of the system during the transition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it covers, the benefit is large and concrete: the Supreme Court's Olmstead decision established a civil right to community living in 1999, but states have not delivered it, and this bill would put an enforceable right, timelines, reporting, and money behind that promise [S3]. The costs are real but targeted at states, insurers, and institutional providers rather than at the people being served; the main honest criticism is that the federal government mandates the transition without fully funding it, leaving states to close the gap over 12 years.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees in each, and neither took it further before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced May 16, 2017 by Rep. Sensenbrenner and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees [S1] [S5].
It gathered 144 cosponsors, 124 Democrats and 20 Republicans [S4].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health on May 19, 2017 and to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice on June 7, 2017, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action afterward [S5].
The 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019, and the bill expired without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that would have been required to shift long-term care funding out of institutions, and the institutional care industry that depends on that funding, are better off because the bill never moved. Disabled people who need community-based services gained nothing from this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 124 Democrats and 20 Republicans signed on — but the bill never reached a vote, so no recorded vote shows where each party stood.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care providers
industries.note: The bill requires states to shift Medicaid funding from institutional settings to home and community-based services, which would move revenue away from facilities that profit from keeping people in institutions. Its interest in the status quo runs against disabled people's right to live at home.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and home care workers
industries.note: The bill requires payment rates sufficient to ensure a workforce able to support people in the community, expanding demand for home-based care and the workers who provide it.

As 'LTSS insurance providers' they would face the same nondiscrimination rules as governments — no waiting lists, cost caps, or forced congregate settings — and would have to fund community-based services for enrollees who qualify for institutional placement.

States gain a five-point federal Medicaid match increase for compliant home and community spending but must carry out a 12-year transition plan, self-evaluations, annual reporting, and expanded accessible housing.
